body: Also reproducible on 4.5.0 stable and 4.7 dev 4

I can reproduce the same issue in GodotPhysics as well. The issue is that:

* GD script creates a `SphereShape3D`, this creates a `JoltSphereShape` internally
* It sets the default radius to 0.5 and schedules it to be applied to the `JoltSphereShape3D` through the multi thread physics server wrapper's `PhysicsServer3DWrapMT::command_queue` (via `PhysicsServer3DWrapMT::shape_set_data`)
* GD script sets the radius to 1.0 and again schedules the change on the `command_queue`
* Now the script calls `world.direct_space_state` which ends up in `PhysicsServer3DWrapMT::space_get_direct_state`. This returns the regular (non multi thread safe) `JoltPhysicsServer3D`.
* The script calls `get_rest_info` which calls `JoltSphereShape3D::_build`. The `command_queue` hasn't been processed yet, so the `JoltSphereShape3D::radius` is still 0. This prints the error and fails to create the Jolt SphereShape.
* Since no SphereShape is created, the collision test fails and an empty `result` is returned.
* Later the `command_queue` is flushed and the radius is set correctly, but that is unfortunately too late.

I can fix the issue by changing this:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/3f63a400fa8f454b09f12201152025c1805b3df5/servers/physics_3d/physics_server_3d_wrap_mt.h#L121-L124

into this:

```C++
PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D *space_get_direct_state(RID p_space) override {
	ERR_FAIL_COND_V(!Thread::is_main_thread(), nullptr);
	command_queue.flush_all(); // Ensure that all modifications have been written before returning the direct state
	return physics_server_3d->space_get_direct_state(p_space);
}
```

but that makes the main thread block until the physics thread has processed all changes. It has the potential to:

* Create a bottleneck
* Create deadlocks (which I've seen happen in other reported issues relating to `PhysicsServer3DWrapMT`, I'm not sure if it would happen for this case)

Several workarounds are possible. They all boil down to ensuring that the `SphereShape3D` is created at least 1 physics step before using it. You can either make it part of the node tree or you can create it earlier in the script.

Can confirm the same issue affects `CapsuleShape3D` under Jolt Physics as well. Both `height` and `radius` default to `0`:

```
E 0:00:00:768   node_3d.gd:13 @ _physics_process(): Failed to build Jolt Physics capsule shape with {height=0.000000 radius=0.000000}. Its radius must be greater than 0. This shape belongs to '<unknown>' and 0 other object(s).
  <C++ Error>   Condition "radius <= 0.0f" is true. Returning: nullptr
  <C++ Source>  modules/jolt_physics/shapes/jolt_capsule_shape_3d.cpp:38 @ _build()
  <Stack Trace> node_3d.gd:13 @ _physics_process()

```
```
E 0:00:00:768   node_3d.gd:13 @ _physics_process(): Parameter "jolt_shape" is null.
  <C++ Source>  modules/jolt_physics/spaces/jolt_physics_direct_space_state_3d.cpp:737 @ rest_info()
  <Stack Trace> node_3d.gd:13 @ _physics_process()
```

Interestingly, this does **not** reproduce with GodotPhysics3D for `CapsuleShape3D`. And `CylinderShape3D` doesn't throw with either backend.

Godot physics does not have any error handling for doing a collision check with a capsule of `radius = 0` or `height = 0` so it may appear to work, but it is not. Try to adjust your scene so that only a shape with the correct height and radius would report a collision and I think you'll see that it will no longer report a collision.

> Godot physics does not have any error handling for doing a collision check with a capsule of `radius = 0` or `height = 0` so it may appear to work, but it is not. Try to adjust your scene so that only a shape with the correct height and radius would report a collision and I think you'll see that it will no longer report a collision.

You're right, GodotPhysics3D silently fails for `CapsuleShape3D` as well with no error and just an empty result. Same for `CylinderShape3D`.

This is a duplicate of #109213. There is a fix pending (#117268) but ideally it would get a proper review first.

Obviously the performance implications of that fix are not great, but I'd rather fix this correctness issue first and try to claw back performance later (if at all possible).

Since you've familiarized yourself with the issue a bit @jrouwe, a review from you would go a long way to getting it merged, assuming you don't prefer the PR it supersedes (#116897) or some other alternative approach.

> you would still be able to shoot yourself in the foot by getting the direct space state before creating the shape

Oh right, good point. Not sure how I missed that scenario when discussing #116897.

> These would route all calls to the underlying `PhysicsDirectBodyState3D` / `PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D` objects (just like `PhysicsServer3DWrapMT`) preceeded by `command_queue.flush_if_pending()` or by using `command_queue.push_and_sync(...)` to run the work on the physics thread. `body_test_motion` will need similar treatment.

I'm not a huge fan of having queries prompt a flush to begin with. As talked about in #116897, query nodes like `RayCast3D` calls the actual `intersect_ray` as part of `NOTIFICATION_INTERNAL_PHYSICS_PROCESS`, which is sent through the scene tree after `_physics_process`, but before `PhysicsServer3D::end_sync`, and since most commands will likely be queued up in `_physics_process`, a single `RayCast3D` node anywhere in the scene tree will more or less guarantee serial processing of every single command.

Perhaps it's a questionable stance on my part, but I see this kind of performance volatility as more problematic (and harder to develop for) than just immediately processing everything but the physics step. And that's assuming anyone ends up processing any significant amount of commands in parallel at all, which might not be a given, considering how prevalent physics queries are in games.

I can't say I have any other ideas off the top of my head though.

Yeah you're right. If you're not doing any ray casts then queuing things in the way I described would be a win, but as soon as you start querying it could very well be a net loss due to having to wait for the physics thread to wake up and execute the command queue.

Another option would be to introduce a new mutex on `PhysicsServer3DWrapMT` which controls access to the underlying `PhysicsServer3D` and all of its components. You'd still have `PhysicsDirectBodyState3DWrapMT` and `PhysicsDirectBodyState3DWrapMT` to guard access but the approach would be:

* Any function that doesn't need an immediate result gets queued and the physics thread gets woken up (or perhaps we only do this for functions that we know are expensive or when we already have items in the queue)
* Any function that does need a result locks the mutex, flushes the queue (executes work on the current thread) and then runs the function
* The physics thread would need to lock the mutex before picking up an item from the queue to avoid race conditions

This would mean that if the physics thread is busy, the other (let's call it 'main') thread will need to wait for it to complete, but if the physics thread is not busy then the main thread can immediately do the work without going through the command queue. The only risk I see here is that if you alternate between 'function without return value' and 'function with return value' that you risk ping ponging the mutex between the physics and main thread which would incur some overhead. For any other pattern, the main thread would be able to continue longer before stalling and the physics thread could start executing work in parallel.

It sounds like that wouldn't be all that different from what we had before #109591, but with the important distinction of having the `PhysicsDirect*State3DWrapMT` classes, to prevent the problematic race conditions that prompted that change to begin with.

I'd say it's probably the more realistic option. I likely won't have time to explore it myself any time soon though.
